extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, poets, editors, and public speakers (general literary readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive, essayistic guidance on writing (especially verse), publication, lecturing, and editorial duties—aimed at helping aspiring authors, poets, and editors understand good practice and common pitfalls. Contains admonitions about premature publication, editorial responsibility, authenticity in public performance, and how to give/receive criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry must be worth writing to justify public attention
rubrics_metrics.description: “A young man can get rid of the presumption against him afforded by his writing verses only by convincing us that they are verses worth writing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied standard: mere activity in writing verse creates a presumption of vanity unless the work itself demonstrates value. The passage frames quality as the only way to overcome social skepticism about young poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make verse an incidental occupation and delay printing
rubrics_metrics.description: “writing verse should be an incidental occupation only, not interfering with the hoe, the needle, the lapstone, or the ledger,—and, above all that there should be no hurry in printing what is written.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice: do not let writing crowd out practical work; avoid rushing to publish. The author recommends study of good models and restraint in issuing printed work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premature publication fosters delusion in inferior writers (anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The poetaster who has tasted type is done for. He is like the man who has once been a candidate for the Presidency. He feeds on the madder of his delusion all his days...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: once an untalented writer experiences publication ('tastes type'), they may become permanently self-deluded. Anti-pattern: encouragement of early, undeserved publication leads to lifelong vanity and lowered standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: When asked for an opinion, expect the seeker wants praise
rubrics_metrics.description: “You may set it down as a truth which admits of few exceptions, that those who ask your _opinion_ really want your _praise_, and will be contented with nothing less.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social/evaluative norm for critics and advisors: recognize the emotional motive behind requests for critique; temper candor with kindness and realistic expectations about how frank judgments will be received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors owe the public the best content they can provide
rubrics_metrics.description: “An editor is a person under a contract with the public to furnish them with the best things he can afford for his money.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial duty: prioritize readers and quality over private sympathy. The author argues editors must develop 'enormous calluses' and reject unfit productions despite personal inclinations to help authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish inferior work as charity (editorial anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Charity shown by the publication of an inferior article would be like the generosity of Claude Duval ... who pitied the poor so much they robbed the rich to have the means of relieving them.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing inferior pieces as 'charity' harms the public and corrupts standards. The metaphor underscores that well-intentioned generosity is inappropriate when it degrades the publication's quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: When appealed to help needy writers, editors must still reject unfit submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Account of appeals made 'in behalf of some person in needy circumstances who wishes to make a living by the pen' and the admonition that editors must reject deficient manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural/practical standard: compassionate motives do not override the editor's contractual obligation to readers. The passage reinforces that charity in publication is misapplied and that one 'cannot burn his house down to warm the hands' of the needy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity in public speaking and lecturing is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: “If a man shows himself other than he is, if he belittles himself before an audience for hire, then he acts unworthily. But a true word, fresh from the lips of a true man, is worth paying for...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norm for authors who lecture: it is acceptable and honorable to be paid for authentic self-expression; the vice is in acting a false or belittled persona to earn money. Distinguishes between genuine performance and self-degradation for hire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious and devotional writing should display gentlemanly breeding
rubrics_metrics.description: “A man should be a gentleman in his hymns and prayers; the fondness for ‘scenes,’ among vulgar saints, contrasts so meanly with that—”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic criterion: one’s religious writing reveals one’s breeding; avoid vulgar theatrics in devotional contexts. The author uses examples of admired devotional poems to show how tasteful expression elevates religious sentiment.
